mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array by its index?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Arrays are stored in contiguous memory locations. Because the size of each element is constant, the memory address of any element can be calculated directly using the formula: Base Address + (Index * Size of Element). Since this calculation takes the same amount of time regardless of the array's size, the time complexity is constant, or O(1).

mcq_data.question: In a singly linked list, what is the time complexity to delete a node given only a pointer to that node (not the head)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: If you have a pointer to the node to be deleted, you can copy the data from the next node into the current node and then delete the next node by adjusting the 'next' pointer. This 'trick' takes constant time. However, note that this doesn't work for the last node in the list. Generally, in a theoretical sense for a middle node, it is O(1).

mcq_data.question: Which data structure follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle. This means the last element added to the stack will be the first one to be removed. Common operations include Push (add) and Pop (remove). Examples include undo mechanisms in editors and function call stacks in recursion.

mcq_data.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an element in a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: While a balanced BST offers O(log n) search time, the worst-case scenario occurs when the tree becomes 'skewed' (essentially looking like a linked list). In a skewed tree, you may have to traverse all N nodes to find the target or determine it's not there, resulting in O(n) complexity.

mcq_data.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms is stable and has a worst-case time complexity of O(n log n)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases (best, average, and worst). It is also 'stable,' meaning it preserves the relative order of equal elements. Quick Sort is often faster in practice but has a worst-case of O(n^2) and is not inherently stable.

mcq_data.question: Which tree traversal visits the nodes in the order: Left, Root, Right?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree first, then the root node, and finally the right subtree. In a Binary Search Tree (BST), an in-order traversal results in the elements being visited in non-decreasing (sorted) order.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is typically used to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) on a graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: BFS explores the neighbor nodes first before moving to the next level neighbors. A Queue (FIFO) is used to keep track of the nodes discovered but not yet visited. When a node is visited, all its unvisited neighbors are added to the back of the queue.

mcq_data.question: What is a 'collision' in a Hash Table?

options.A: When two different keys produce the same hash value
options.B: When the hash table runs out of memory
options.C: When a key is deleted from the table
options.D: When the hash function returns a negative value

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A collision occurs when two distinct keys are mapped to the same index by the hash function. Since a single index can usually hold only one piece of data in a simple array, strategies like Chaining (using linked lists) or Open Addressing (finding another empty slot) are used to resolve these conflicts.

mcq_data.question: In a circular queue implemented using an array of size 'n', how is the 'next' position of the rear pointer calculated?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In a circular queue, when the pointer reaches the end of the array, it needs to wrap around to the beginning (index 0). The modulo operator (%) is used for this. If 'rear' is at index n-1, (n-1 + 1) % n equals 0, correctly pointing to the start of the array.

mcq_data.question: What is the prerequisite for performing a Binary Search on a list?

options.C: The list must be implemented as a Linked List
options.D: The list must contain only integers

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Binary Search works on the principle of divide and conquer by comparing the target value to the middle element. This logic only works if the list is sorted. If the target is smaller than the middle, you search the left half; if larger, the right half. Without sorting, this elimination is impossible.

mcq_data.question: What is the space complexity of a recursive function that calculates the Nth Fibonacci number without memoization?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The space complexity of a recursive function is determined by the maximum depth of the recursion stack. To calculate Fib(n), the call stack reaches a depth of 'n' before it starts returning. Even though the time complexity is exponential O(2^n), the space complexity (stack depth) is linear O(n).

mcq_data.question: In a Max-Heap implemented as an array, if a node is at index 'i', what is the index of its left child?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: For a zero-indexed array representation of a binary heap, the left child of a node at index 'i' is always at '2i + 1', and the right child is at '2i + 2'. The parent of a node at index 'i' can be found at '(i - 1) / 2'.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is used to find the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with no negative edge weights?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Dijkstra's Algorithm is a greedy algorithm used for finding the shortest paths between nodes in a graph. It works specifically for graphs with non-negative weights. If the graph has negative weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead.

mcq_data.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly picks the smallest element from the unsorted part and puts it at the beginning?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Selection Sort works by maintaining two sub-arrays: one already sorted and the other unsorted. In every iteration, the minimum element from the unsorted sub-array is picked and moved to the sorted sub-array. It has a time complexity of O(n^2) in all cases.

mcq_data.question: What is the main advantage of a doubly linked list over a singly linked list?

options.B: Faster access to elements by index
options.C: Can be traversed in both directions

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A doubly linked list contains an extra pointer ('prev') in each node pointing to the previous node. This allows for bidirectional traversal (forward and backward). However, this comes at the cost of extra memory for the additional pointer.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is most efficient for implementing a 'Priority Queue' where elements are retrieved based on importance?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A Binary Heap (Min-Heap or Max-Heap) is the most efficient structure for a Priority Queue. It allows for O(log n) insertion and O(log n) removal of the highest/lowest priority element, while keeping the structure balanced. A sorted array would take O(n) for insertion.

mcq_data.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 'h'? (Assume root is at height 0)
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A full binary tree at height 0 has 1 node (2^1 - 1). At height 1, it has 3 nodes (2^2 - 1). The formula for the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 'h' is 2^(h+1) - 1.

mcq_data.question: If an algorithm's time complexity is O(n log n), and the input size doubles, by approximately what factor does the running time increase?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: If we replace 'n' with '2n', the new time is 2n * log(2n), which is 2n * (log n + log 2) = 2n log n + 2n. This is slightly more than double the original time (2 * n log n). This makes O(n log n) very efficient compared to O(n^2).

mcq_data.question: In hash table 'Open Addressing', what is 'Linear Probing'?

options.B: Searching for the next available slot sequentially
options.C: Creating a linked list at the hash index

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Linear Probing is a collision resolution technique where, if a collision occurs at index 'i', the algorithm checks index i+1, i+2, i+3, and so on, until an empty slot is found. This can lead to 'primary clustering' where blocks of occupied slots build up.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of Depth-First Search (DFS) on a graph represented by an Adjacency List (where V = vertices, E = edges)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In an adjacency list, DFS visits every vertex once (V) and explores every edge once (E) for directed graphs (or twice for undirected). Thus, the total time complexity is O(V + E). If an Adjacency Matrix were used, it would be O(V^2).

mcq_data.question: Which of these is a 'Divide and Conquer' algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Quick Sort is a Divide and Conquer algorithm. It picks an element as a 'pivot' and partitions the given array around the picked pivot. It then recursively sorts the sub-arrays. Merge Sort is another famous example of this paradigm.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is best suited for implementing an 'Undo' feature in a text editor?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The 'Undo' feature requires accessing the most recent action first. This perfectly matches the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) property of a Stack. Every time an action is performed, it is pushed onto the stack. When 'Undo' is pressed, the top action is popped and reversed.

mcq_data.question: In a Binary Search Tree, which node is the 'Successor' of a node 'X' with a right child?

options.B: The rightmost node in the left subtree of X
options.C: The leftmost node in the right subtree of X

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The in-order successor of a node is the node with the smallest key greater than the key of the input node. If a node has a right subtree, the successor is the minimum element in that right subtree, which is found by going to the right child and then following the 'left' pointers as far as possible.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of the following code snippet: `for(int i=1; i<n; i=i*2) { ... }`?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The loop variable 'i' doubles in each iteration (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...). This means the number of iterations 'k' is the power to which 2 must be raised to reach 'n' (2^k = n). Solving for k gives k = log2(n), hence the complexity is O(log n).

mcq_data.question: What is a 'Cycle' in a graph?

options.A: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex
options.B: A graph where every node is connected to every other node
options.C: A node with no incoming edges
options.D: An edge that connects a node to itself

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A cycle in a graph is a non-empty path in which the only repeated vertices are the first and last vertices. In simple terms, if you can start at a node and follow a path of edges to get back to the same node without reusing an edge, the graph contains a cycle.

mcq_data.question: Which of the following growth rates is the slowest?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Logarithmic growth O(log n) is much slower (and therefore better for large data) than linear O(n), log-linear O(n log n), or exponential O(2^n). For example, if n=1,000,000, log(n) is roughly 20, while n is 1,000,000.

mcq_data.question: What happens if you try to 'Pop' from an empty stack?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Underflow is a condition that occurs when you attempt to remove or 'pop' an item from a data structure that is already empty. Conversely, 'Overflow' happens when you try to 'push' an item into a data structure (like an array-based stack) that has reached its maximum capacity.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity to 'Heapify' an array of size 'n' to build a heap?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Although inserting 'n' elements into a heap one by one takes O(n log n), the 'Build-Heap' operation (Heapify) can be performed in O(n) time by starting from the last non-leaf nodes and working up to the root. This is a common point of confusion in DSA exams.

mcq_data.question: In an AVL tree, what is the maximum allowed difference between the heights of left and right subtrees for any node?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree. The 'Balance Factor' for any node is calculated as (height of left subtree - height of right subtree). In an AVL tree, this factor must be -1, 0, or 1. If it deviates, rotations are performed to rebalance the tree.

mcq_data.question: Which sorting algorithm is often used in practice for small arrays or as part of a hybrid algorithm (like Timsort)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Insertion Sort is very efficient for small datasets and nearly sorted arrays. Because of its low overhead, modern hybrid sorting algorithms like Timsort (used in Python and Java) use Insertion Sort when the sub-arrays become small enough during the merge process.

Topics include Breadth-First Search (BFS), Depth-First Search (DFS), Dijkstra's Algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Prim's, Kruskal's, and Topological Sorting. Each question includes a detailed explanation to help you understand the 'why' behind the 'how'. Perfect for students and professionals preparing for competitive programming or FAANG interviews.
youtube_metadata.tags: Graph Algorithms, Data Structures, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Kruskal's, Prim's, Topological Sort, Coding Interview, DSA Prep, Programming Quiz

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is typically used to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores the neighbor nodes first, before moving to the next level neighbors. To maintain this 'level-order' exploration, a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure is required. A Queue ensures that nodes are processed in the exact order they were discovered, which is essential for finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

mcq_data.question: Which search algorithm uses a Stack or Recursion to explore as far as possible along each branch before backtracking?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Depth-First Search (DFS) follows a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) pattern. By using a Stack (or the implicit call stack in recursion), the algorithm dives deep into a graph's branches. It only backtracks when it reaches a node with no unvisited neighbors. This makes it ideal for tasks like topological sorting or finding strongly connected components.

mcq_data.question: In a directed graph, the presence of which type of edge during a DFS traversal indicates a cycle?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: During a DFS traversal, a 'Back Edge' connects a vertex to one of its ancestors in the DFS tree. If you encounter an edge $(u, v)$ where $v$ is currently in the recursion stack (an ancestor), it means there is a path from $v$ to $u$ and now an edge from $u$ to $v$, forming a cycle. Tree, Forward, and Cross edges do not signify cycles in directed graphs.

mcq_data.question: What is the primary reason Dijkstra's algorithm may fail on a graph?

options.B: The graph contains negative weight edges.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Dijkstra's algorithm is a greedy algorithm that assumes once a shortest path to a node is found, it will not be improved. Negative weight edges break this assumption because a longer path of edges could technically result in a smaller total weight if one of those edges is negative. For graphs with negative weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm is required.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm for finding the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) grows the tree by adding the cheapest edge that connects a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside the tree?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Prim's algorithm starts from a single node and greedily expands the spanning tree by choosing the minimum weight edge that connects a visited node to an unvisited node. This contrasts with Kruskal's, which picks the absolute minimum weight edges from the entire graph (provided they don't form a cycle) regardless of whether they are connected to the current growth point.

mcq_data.question: Topological sorting can only be performed on which type of graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A topological sort is a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge $(u, v)$, vertex $u$ comes before $v$. If the graph has a cycle, no such ordering exists. Therefore, the graph must be Directed and Acyclic (DAG). It is widely used in scheduling tasks with dependencies.

mcq_data.question: Which graph representation is more space-efficient for a sparse graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: An Adjacency Matrix requires $O(V^2)$ space regardless of the number of edges. An Adjacency List requires $O(V + E)$ space. In a sparse graph where $E$ is much less than $V^2$, the Adjacency List is significantly more efficient. The Adjacency Matrix is usually preferred only for very dense graphs where $E$ approaches $V^2$.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm uses dynamic programming to find shortest paths between all pairs of vertices. It consists of three nested loops, each iterating over the $V$ vertices. This results in a time complexity of $O(V^3)$. While slow for large graphs, it is simple to implement and handles negative weights (but not negative cycles).

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is most suitable for finding the shortest path in a graph where edge weights represent probabilities (product of weights) rather than sums?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: When dealing with probabilities, we want to maximize the product of weights. Since $\log(a \cdot b) = \log(a) + \log(b)$, we can transform the product problem into a summation problem by taking the negative logarithm of the weights. Once transformed, Dijkstra's algorithm can find the shortest (most probable) path.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is essential for the efficient implementation of Kruskal's algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kruskal's algorithm works by sorting all edges and adding them if they don't form a cycle. To efficiently check if two vertices are in the same component (and thus would form a cycle), we use the Disjoint Set Union (DSU) or Union-Find data structure. With path compression and union by rank, these operations are nearly constant time.

mcq_data.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph with $V$ vertices?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In a simple undirected graph, each pair of distinct vertices can have at most one edge. The number of ways to choose 2 vertices from $V$ is given by the combination formula $\binom{V}{2}$, which is $\frac{V(V-1)}{2}$. For a directed graph, the answer would be $V(V-1)$ because the direction matters.

mcq_data.question: Kosaraju's algorithm for finding Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) involves how many passes of DFS?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kosaraju's algorithm uses two DFS passes. The first pass is on the original graph to determine the 'finishing times' of vertices (pushed onto a stack). The graph is then transposed (all edges reversed). The second DFS pass is performed on the transposed graph in the order of the finishing times from the stack to identify the SCCs.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm can detect the presence of a negative cycle in a graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Bellman-Ford algorithm relaxes all edges $V-1$ times. If a further relaxation is possible on the $V$-th iteration, it indicates that a path's weight can be infinitely decreased, confirming the existence of a negative cycle. Dijkstra's algorithm cannot handle negative weights and thus cannot detect negative cycles.

mcq_data.question: The Ford-Fulkerson method is used to solve which type of problem?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Ford-Fulkerson method (and its implementation via Edmonds-Karp) computes the maximum flow in a flow network. It works by repeatedly finding 'augmenting paths' in the residual graph—paths from source to sink where more flow can be pushed—until no such paths remain.

mcq_data.question: A graph where every pair of distinct vertices is connected by a unique edge is called a:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A Complete Graph, denoted as $K_n$, is a simple undirected graph where every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex. In such a graph, the number of edges is exactly $V(V-1)/2$. A 'Connected Graph' only requires a path to exist between all pairs, not a direct edge.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of both BFS and DFS when using an Adjacency List?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: When using an adjacency list, both algorithms visit every vertex once ($V$) and examine every edge connected to those vertices. Since each edge is examined at most twice (once for each endpoint in an undirected graph), the total time complexity is proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges: $O(V + E)$.

mcq_data.question: An articulation point in an undirected graph is a vertex that, if removed:

options.A: Reduces the number of edges to zero.
options.B: Increases the number of connected components.
options.C: Turns a DAG into a cyclic graph.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Articulation points (or cut vertices) are critical nodes in a graph's connectivity. Removing such a node 'breaks' the graph into more pieces (components) than it originally had. Finding these points is essential for network reliability analysis and can be done in $O(V+E)$ using DFS.

mcq_data.question: A graph is Bipartite if and only if it does not contain a cycle of:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A Bipartite graph is one where vertices can be divided into two independent sets such that every edge connects a vertex from one set to the other. If a graph contains an odd cycle, it's impossible to alternate colors (or sets) around the cycle and return to the start with a valid coloring. Thus, no odd cycles are allowed.

mcq_data.question: In a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), what is the most efficient way to find the shortest path from a single source?

options.C: Topological Sort followed by edge relaxation

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: For DAGs, we can find the shortest path in $O(V+E)$ time by processing vertices in topological order. Since there are no cycles, once we process a vertex, we are guaranteed to have found its shortest path because no subsequent edges can circle back to it. This is faster than Dijkstra's $O(E \log V)$.

mcq_data.question: Handshaking Lemma states that the sum of degrees of all vertices in an undirected graph is equal to:

options.B: Two times the number of edges
options.C: The square of the number of vertices

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Handshaking Lemma arises because every edge $(u, v)$ contributes exactly 1 to the degree of vertex $u$ and exactly 1 to the degree of vertex $v$. Therefore, when you sum all degrees, every edge has been counted exactly twice. $\sum deg(v) = 2|E|$.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is a 'Best-First Search' that uses a heuristic to guide the search towards a target node?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A* Search is an extension of Dijkstra's algorithm that uses $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the cost from the start to node $n$, and $h(n)$ is a heuristic estimate of the cost from $n$ to the goal. This 'informed' search often finds the shortest path much faster than Dijkstra's by focusing on nodes that look promising.

mcq_data.question: A 'Bridge' in an undirected graph is an edge that:

options.C: When removed, increases the number of connected components.
options.D: Connects a leaf node to the rest of the tree.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Similar to an articulation point, a bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph (or a component of it). In a tree, every edge is a bridge. In a cycle, no edge is a bridge. Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm identifies these in $O(V+E)$ time.

mcq_data.question: A tree is a connected graph with how many edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A key property of a tree (a connected acyclic graph) with $V$ vertices is that it must have exactly $V-1$ edges. If it had fewer, it couldn't be connected. If it had more, it would necessarily contain at least one cycle.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is used to find all-pairs shortest paths and can handle negative weights but not negative cycles?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic programming algorithm that considers all possible intermediate vertices to find shortest paths between all pairs. It correctly handles negative edge weights. However, if a negative cycle exists, the shortest path is undefined (it's negative infinity), and the algorithm's diagonal values will become negative.

mcq_data.question: What is the complexity of checking if an edge exists between two vertices $u$ and $v$ in an Adjacency Matrix?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The primary advantage of an Adjacency Matrix is that checking for the existence of an edge $(u, v)$ is a simple array lookup: `matrix[u][v]`. This is an $O(1)$ constant time operation. In an Adjacency List, this check would take $O(degree(u))$, which could be $O(V)$ in the worst case.

mcq_data.question: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting uses which of the following properties of vertices?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kahn's algorithm works by maintaining the 'in-degree' (number of incoming edges) for each vertex. It starts by adding all vertices with an in-degree of 0 (no dependencies) to a queue. As vertices are removed from the queue, the in-degrees of their neighbors are decremented. If a neighbor's in-degree reaches 0, it is added to the queue.

mcq_data.question: How many spanning trees does a complete graph $K_n$ have? (Cayley's Formula)
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Cayley's Formula is a classic result in graph theory stating that for a complete graph with $n$ labeled vertices, there are $n^{n-2}$ distinct spanning trees. For example, for $n=3$, there are $3^{(3-2)} = 3$ spanning trees.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Bellman-Ford algorithm relaxes all $E$ edges in the graph $V-1$ times. This leads to a total time complexity of $O(V \cdot E)$. This is slower than Dijkstra's but more robust as it handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.

mcq_data.question: Can BFS be used to detect a cycle in an undirected graph?

options.B: Yes, if we encounter a previously visited node that is not the parent.
options.C: Yes, only if the graph is weighted.
options.D: No, BFS is only for shortest paths.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In an undirected graph, BFS can detect cycles. During traversal, if we see an adjacent node that has already been visited and is NOT the parent of the current node, it implies there is another path to that node, forming a cycle.

mcq_data.question: Which traversal is guaranteed to find the node closest to the root in an unweighted tree?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: BFS explores nodes level by level. Because it visits all nodes at distance $d$ before any nodes at distance $d+1$, it is guaranteed to find the closest node (shortest path) in any unweighted structure. DFS might go deep into one branch and find a target much further away before ever checking nearby branches.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is most space-efficient for representing a sparse graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: An Adjacency Matrix requires O(V^2) space regardless of the number of edges, which is wasteful for sparse graphs (where E is much smaller than V^2). An Adjacency List only stores existing edges, resulting in a space complexity of O(V + E). This makes it significantly more efficient for networks like social media or road maps where each node is only connected to a few others.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) using an adjacency list representation?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In BFS, every vertex is added to the queue exactly once, contributing O(V). For each vertex, we iterate over its adjacent edges. In an adjacency list, the sum of lengths of all adjacency lists is 2E for undirected graphs and E for directed graphs. Thus, the total time spent looking at edges is O(E). Combining these, the complexity is O(V + E). If an adjacency matrix were used, the complexity would be O(V^2).

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is best suited for finding the shortest path from a single source in a graph that contains negative edge weights but no negative cycles?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Dijkstra's algorithm fails with negative weights because it greedily assumes that once a node is visited, its shortest path is found. Bellman-Ford, however, relaxes all edges V-1 times, allowing it to correctly calculate paths even when weights are negative. While Floyd-Warshall also handles negative weights, it is an All-Pairs algorithm with O(V^3) complexity, making Bellman-Ford (O(V*E)) more efficient for single-source problems.

mcq_data.question: To detect a cycle in a directed graph, which of the following states during DFS indicates a cycle?

options.A: Encountering a node currently in the recursion stack
options.B: Encountering a node already marked as visited
options.D: Reaching a node with no out-degree

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In a directed graph, a cycle exists if and only if a 'back edge' is found during DFS. A back edge connects a vertex to one of its ancestors in the DFS tree. We track this using a 'recursion stack' (or an array keeping track of nodes in the current path). If we encounter a node that is already in the recursion stack, it means we have looped back to an ancestor, confirming a cycle.

mcq_data.question: Prim's algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree is based on which algorithmic paradigm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Prim's algorithm follows the Greedy paradigm. It starts with a single vertex and at each step, it adds the cheapest edge that connects a vertex in the MST to a vertex outside the MST. By making the local optimal choice at each step, it eventually achieves the global optimum (the minimum total weight for a spanning tree).

mcq_data.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph with 'n' vertices?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In a simple undirected graph, each pair of vertices can have at most one edge. The number of ways to choose 2 vertices out of n is given by the combination formula $nC2 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For a directed graph, the answer would be $n(n-1)$ because each pair can have two directed edges (one in each direction).

mcq_data.question: Topological sorting can be performed on which type of graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Topological sorting is a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge $u \to v$, vertex $u$ comes before $v$. This is only possible if there are no cycles. If there is a cycle, no vertex in the cycle can come 'first'. Therefore, it only applies to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).

mcq_data.question: What is the primary advantage of using the Floyd-Warshall algorithm over running Dijkstra's multiple times?

options.A: It is faster for sparse graphs
options.B: It is simpler to implement using dynamic programming and handles negative weights
options.C: It has a lower time complexity than Dijkstra

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Floyd-Warshall is an All-Pairs Shortest Path algorithm with a very simple triply-nested loop structure (O(V^3)). Its main advantage is that it can handle negative edge weights (as long as there are no negative cycles) and is extremely easy to implement. While running Dijkstra V times with a Fibonacci heap is O(V*E + V^2 log V), Floyd-Warshall remains the standard for dense graphs and general weight scenarios.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is typically used to efficiently implement Kruskal's algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kruskal's algorithm works by sorting all edges and adding them one by one if they don't form a cycle. To check if adding an edge $(u, v)$ forms a cycle, we need to know if $u$ and $v$ are already in the same connected component. The Disjoint Set Union (DSU) with path compression and union by rank provides nearly constant time operations for 'Find' and 'Union', making it the ideal choice for this task.

mcq_data.question: In an adjacency matrix of an undirected graph, the matrix is always:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In an undirected graph, if there is an edge between vertex $i$ and vertex $j$, then the entry at $A[i][j]$ is 1 (or the weight) and the entry at $A[j][i]$ is also 1. Because $A[i][j] = A[j][i]$ for all $i, j$, the matrix is symmetric about the main diagonal.

mcq_data.question: Which traversal is used to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: BFS explores nodes level by level. In an unweighted graph, the first time a node is reached, it is guaranteed to be via the shortest path (minimum number of edges) from the source. DFS does not guarantee this, as it may go deep down one path and find a destination much later than a shorter path available at a shallower level.

mcq_data.question: A graph where every vertex has the same degree is called a:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A 'Regular Graph' is defined specifically by the property that all vertices have the same degree. For example, a 3-regular graph is one where every node has exactly 3 edges. A Complete Graph is a specific type of regular graph where every node has degree $n-1$.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Bellman-Ford consists of an outer loop that runs $V-1$ times. Inside this loop, it iterates over all $E$ edges to perform the relaxation step. This results in a total time complexity of $O((V-1) * E)$, which is simplified to $O(V * E)$.

mcq_data.question: What is a 'Strongly Connected Component' (SCC) in a directed graph?

options.A: A subset of vertices where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex in that subset
options.B: A subset where every vertex has an edge to every other vertex
options.C: A component that remains connected after removing any one edge
options.D: A tree that spans all vertices

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In a directed graph, an SCC is a maximal subgraph where for every pair of vertices $(u, v)$, there is a path from $u$ to $v$ AND a path from $v$ to $u$. Algorithms like Tarjan's or Kosaraju's are used to find these components in $O(V+E)$ time.

mcq_data.question: A bipartite graph can be colored with how many colors such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The definition of a bipartite graph is that its vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets such that every edge connects a vertex in one set to a vertex in the other. Therefore, you only need 2 colors—one for each set—to satisfy the coloring condition. If a graph contains an odd cycle, it is NOT bipartite.

mcq_data.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is essentially a generalization of:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph by exploring neighbors level by level. Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue instead of a standard queue to explore neighbors based on 'accumulated weight' rather than just 'hop count', making it a generalization of BFS for weighted graphs.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm is used to find the Transitive Closure of a graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Transitive closure determines if there is a path between every pair of vertices $(i, j)$. The Floyd-Warshall algorithm can be easily adapted for this by using boolean OR instead of addition and 'exists' instead of distance, effectively filling the reachability matrix in $O(V^3)$.

mcq_data.question: What is the Handshaking Lemma in graph theory?

options.A: The number of vertices with odd degree is always even
options.B: The sum of degrees is equal to the number of edges
options.C: Every graph has at least one cycle
options.D: A graph with n vertices has n-1 edges

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Handshaking Lemma states that the sum of the degrees of all vertices in a graph is twice the number of edges ($2E$). Since $2E$ is always even, the sum of degrees must be even. This mathematically implies that there must be an even number of vertices with an odd degree.

mcq_data.question: Using Union-Find for cycle detection is most applicable to which type of graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Union-Find is excellent for detecting cycles in undirected graphs. As we process edges $(u, v)$, we check if $u$ and $v$ belong to the same set. If they do, adding $(u, v)$ completes a cycle. It is not directly applicable to directed graphs because the direction matters for cycle formation (a path must exist in a specific orientation).

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of checking if an edge exists between two vertices in an adjacency matrix?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In an adjacency matrix, we can directly access the element at `matrix[i][j]`. This is an array indexing operation, which takes constant time, $O(1)$. In contrast, an adjacency list would require traversing the list of vertex $i$, which takes $O(\text{degree of } i)$.

mcq_data.question: In Kruskal's algorithm, why do we sort the edges?

options.A: To ensure we visit all vertices
options.B: To pick the smallest weight edge first (Greedy approach)
options.C: To avoid using a Disjoint Set

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kruskal's is a greedy algorithm. By sorting edges from lowest to highest weight, we ensure that we always try to include the cheapest possible connections first, which is the core logic required to minimize the total weight of the spanning tree.

mcq_data.question: An Euler Path exists in an undirected connected graph if and only if:

options.B: Exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: An Euler Path is a trail that visits every edge exactly once. For this to be possible, the 'start' and 'end' nodes can have odd degrees (one edge to leave/enter), but all 'middle' nodes must have even degrees to ensure every entry into the node has a corresponding exit. If 0 nodes are odd, it's an Euler Circuit; if exactly 2 are odd, it's an Euler Path.

mcq_data.question: The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm is used to solve which problem?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm calculates the maximum flow in a flow network. It works by repeatedly finding 'augmenting paths' in a residual graph and increasing the flow until no more paths from source to sink exist. It is intrinsically linked to the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of building an adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: To build an adjacency matrix, you must first initialize a $V 	imes V$ matrix with zeros, which takes $O(V^2)$ time. Then, you iterate through the $E$ edges to set the appropriate cells, which takes $O(E)$. Since $E$ is at most $V^2$, the overall complexity is dominated by $O(V^2)$.

mcq_data.question: Kahn's algorithm is used for:
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kahn's algorithm is a popular BFS-based approach for Topological Sorting. It works by maintaining the in-degree of all vertices, adding vertices with in-degree 0 to a queue, and iteratively removing them from the graph while updating the in-degrees of their neighbors.

mcq_data.question: An articulation point in a graph is a vertex that, when removed:

options.A: Reduces the number of edges by half
options.B: Increases the number of connected components
options.D: Turns the graph into a tree

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Articulation points (or cut vertices) are critical nodes in a network. Removing such a node disconnects the graph (or a component of it), thereby increasing the total number of connected components. These are often found using a modified DFS algorithm that tracks discovery and 'low' times.

mcq_data.question: A tree with N vertices has how many edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: By definition, a tree is a connected acyclic graph. One of the fundamental properties of a tree is that it always contains exactly $N-1$ edges. If it had more, there would be a cycle; if it had fewer, it would be disconnected.

mcq_data.question: Which data structure is typically used for implementing Depth-First Search (DFS)?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: DFS explores a path as far as possible before backtracking. This 'Last-In, First-Out' behavior is naturally handled by a Stack. This can be either an explicit stack data structure or the implicit call stack provided by recursion.

mcq_data.question: In Dijkstra's algorithm, what happens if we use a Fibonacci Heap instead of a Binary Heap for the priority queue?

options.B: The time complexity improves to $O(E + V \log V)$
options.D: The algorithm fails to find the shortest path

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A Fibonacci Heap has a better amortized time complexity for the 'decrease-key' operation ($O(1)$ compared to $O(\log V)$ for binary heaps). Since Dijkstra's performs $V$ 'extract-min' and up to $E$ 'decrease-key' operations, the complexity drops from $O((V+E) \log V)$ to $O(E + V \log V)$, which is a significant improvement for dense graphs.

mcq_data.question: Which of these is NOT a real-world application of graph algorithms?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Sorting a list of numbers is a linear data structure problem typically solved with comparison or distribution-based algorithms like QuickSort or MergeSort. GPS (Shortest Path), Social Media (Connectivity/Clustering), and Compilers (Topological Sort for dependencies) are all classic applications of graph theory.

youtube_metadata.youtubetitle: DSA Greedy Algorithms Practice Questions and Detailed Solutions for Coding Interviews
youtube_metadata.description:
Master Greedy Algorithms with this comprehensive practice guide. This video covers 30 essential questions focusing on key concepts like fractional knapsack, interval scheduling, and minimum spanning trees. Each question includes a detailed explanation to help you understand the 'why' behind the 'how'. Perfect for students and professionals preparing for technical rounds at top tech companies.

Key topics covered:
- Greedy Choice Property
- Optimal Substructure
- Huffman Coding
- Dijkstra’s Algorithm
- Minimum Spanning Trees (Prim's & Kruskal's)
- Job Sequencing and Activity Selection
youtube_metadata.tags: DSA, Greedy Algorithms, Data Structures, Algorithms, Coding Interview, Huffman Coding, Kruskal's Algorithm, Prim's Algorithm, Dijkstra's, Programming, Tech Interview Prep
mostsearchedongoogle: Difference between Greedy and Dynamic Programming
Pros and cons of greedy algorithms

mcq_data.question: Which of the following properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be applicable?

options.B: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
options.C: Greedy choice property and overlapping subproblems
options.D: Exponential time complexity and recursive structure

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A greedy algorithm works if the problem exhibits two main properties: the Greedy Choice Property (a global optimum can be reached by choosing a local optimum) and Optimal Substructure (an optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems). Overlapping subproblems are a characteristic of Dynamic Programming, not necessarily a requirement for Greedy approaches.

mcq_data.question: In the Fractional Knapsack problem, what is the primary criteria used to sort items before selection?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Greedy strategy for the Fractional Knapsack problem involves calculating the value/weight ratio (profit density) for each item. By sorting items in descending order of this ratio, we ensure that we are utilizing the knapsack's capacity by taking the most 'valuable' items per unit of space first, which leads to the global maximum profit.

mcq_data.question: In Huffman Coding, what type of tree is used to represent the characters?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Huffman coding generates a Full Binary Tree (also known as a proper binary tree), where every internal node has exactly two children. This is because the algorithm merges the two smallest frequency nodes at each step to create a new parent node until only one root remains. This structure ensures that no code is a prefix of another.

mcq_data.question: Which greedy algorithm is specifically designed to find the shortest path from a single source to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Dijkstra's Algorithm is a classic greedy algorithm that finds the shortest path from a starting node to all other nodes in a graph. It works by maintaining a set of visited nodes and repeatedly choosing the unvisited node with the smallest known distance from the source. Note that it fails if the graph contains negative edge weights.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of Kruskal's algorithm using a Union-Find data structure with path compression and union by rank?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kruskal's algorithm involves sorting all edges, which takes O(E log E) time. The Union-Find operations (Union and Find) take almost constant time, specifically O(E α(V)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function. Since log E is dominant over α(V), and E can be at most V^2 (making log E roughly 2 log V), the complexity is typically expressed as O(E log E) or O(E log V).

mcq_data.question: To maximize the number of activities in the Activity Selection problem, how should the activities be sorted?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The optimal greedy strategy for the Activity Selection problem is to always pick the next activity whose finish time is the earliest among the remaining activities. This leaves as much room as possible for subsequent activities. Sorting by finish time ensures that the resource is freed up as quickly as possible.

mcq_data.question: In Job Sequencing with Deadlines, if we have 'n' jobs and each job takes 1 unit of time, what is the best strategy to maximize profit?

options.A: Sort by deadline and pick the first ones
options.B: Sort by profit and assign each job to the latest available slot before its deadline
options.C: Sort by profit and assign to the earliest available slot
options.D: Sort by the ratio of profit/deadline

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The greedy approach for Job Sequencing is to sort jobs in descending order of profit. For each job, try to schedule it as late as possible (at its deadline or just before). This greedy 'late' scheduling leaves earlier slots open for jobs with earlier deadlines, thereby maximizing the total profit.

mcq_data.question: What is the main advantage of Huffman Coding over fixed-length encoding?

options.B: It reduces the average number of bits per character
options.C: It eliminates the need for a frequency table
options.D: It uses more bits for frequent characters to ensure clarity

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Huffman Coding is a variable-length encoding scheme. It assigns shorter binary codes to characters that appear more frequently and longer codes to those that appear less frequently. This results in a reduction of the overall total bits required to store or transmit the data, making it an optimal prefix code.

mcq_data.question: Why does the greedy approach fail for the 0/1 Knapsack problem but work for the Fractional Knapsack problem?

options.B: In 0/1 Knapsack, a local optimal choice does not necessarily lead to a global optimum
options.C: Fractional Knapsack requires sorting, while 0/1 Knapsack does not
options.D: 0/1 Knapsack is a simpler problem that requires recursion

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In 0/1 Knapsack, you cannot take fractions of an item. If you pick an item with the highest profit density, it might take up so much space that you cannot fit other items that would have collectively yielded more profit. Because of this 'all-or-nothing' constraint, the local greedy choice may leave empty space that cannot be filled optimally, requiring Dynamic Programming to explore all combinations.

mcq_data.question: Prim's Algorithm is most efficient when implemented with which data structure for a dense graph?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: For a dense graph where E is approximately V^2, Prim's algorithm using an Adjacency Matrix and a simple array to find the minimum weight edge takes O(V^2) time. Using a binary heap with an adjacency list takes O(E log V). In a dense graph, V^2 is better than V^2 log V. However, for sparse graphs, the heap implementation is preferred.

mcq_data.question: Which of these is a 'top-down' approach where we make a sequence of choices to reach an optimal solution?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Greedy Method is considered a top-down approach because it makes a decision at the current step and then moves on to the remaining subproblem. Unlike Dynamic Programming, which often builds up solutions from the bottom (solving all subproblems first), Greedy makes a choice immediately and never reconsiders it.

mcq_data.question: In Kruskal's algorithm, what is the purpose of the 'Find' operation in the Disjoint Set Union (DSU)?

options.A: To find the shortest edge in the graph
options.B: To determine which component a vertex belongs to and check for cycles
options.C: To find the parent of the root node
options.D: To calculate the total weight of the MST

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In Kruskal's algorithm, we add edges one by one in increasing order of weight. Before adding an edge (u, v), we must ensure it doesn't form a cycle. The 'Find' operation determines the representative (or root) of the sets containing u and v. If Find(u) == Find(v), they are in the same component, and adding the edge would create a cycle.

mcq_data.question: Given frequencies: A: 5, B: 9, C: 12, D: 13, E: 16, F: 45. What is the length of the Huffman code for character 'F'?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In Huffman coding, characters with the highest frequency are placed closest to the root. If you build the tree, F (45) will be one child of the root, and the combination of all other letters (summing to 55) will be the other child. Thus, F is reached in just 1 step from the root, giving it a 1-bit code.

mcq_data.question: What happens if you apply Dijkstra's algorithm to a graph with negative edge weights but no negative cycles?

options.A: It will always find the correct shortest path
options.B: It will crash or enter an infinite loop
options.C: It may produce incorrect results because it assumes once a node is visited, its shortest path is found
options.D: It will only work if the negative edges are at the end of the path

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Dijkstra's is a greedy algorithm that assumes adding an edge can only increase (or keep same) the path length. If negative weights exist, a previously 'closed' node might have its distance reduced by a later path, but Dijkstra's won't revisit it. This is why Bellman-Ford (which is not greedy) is used for graphs with negative weights.

mcq_data.question: For which of the following coin denominations will a greedy algorithm always give the optimal solution for the change-making problem?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The greedy algorithm (always taking the largest coin possible) works for 'canonical' coin systems, like the US currency system {1, 5, 10, 25}. For other sets like {1, 3, 4}, to make 6 cents, Greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins), while the optimal is 3+3 (2 coins).

mcq_data.question: A Matroid is a mathematical structure that generalizes the concept of linear independence. Which algorithm type is guaranteed to find an optimal solution for problems that can be modeled as a Matroid?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Rado-Edmonds Theorem states that a greedy algorithm correctly solves an optimization problem if and only if the underlying structure is a Matroid. Examples include finding the Minimum Spanning Tree (Graphic Matroid) and various scheduling problems.

mcq_data.question: In Fractional Knapsack, if multiple items have the same profit-to-weight ratio, which one should be picked first?

options.A: The one with the smaller weight
options.B: The one with the higher total profit
options.C: It doesn't matter; any of them can be picked
options.D: The one with the higher total weight

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Since you can take any fraction of the items, if the profit density (value per unit weight) is the same, the total profit gained per unit of capacity used is identical regardless of which item you pick. Therefore, the order among items with tied ratios does not affect the final optimal value.

mcq_data.question: A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a graph with V vertices must have how many edges?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: By definition, a tree with V vertices must have exactly V - 1 edges to be connected and acyclic. If it has fewer, it is disconnected. If it has more, it must contain at least one cycle. This rule applies to any spanning tree, including the Minimum Spanning Tree.

mcq_data.question: If a character 'X' has a frequency that is greater than the sum of all other character frequencies, what will be the length of its Huffman code?

options.A: Varies based on the number of characters

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: If the frequency of 'X' is greater than the sum of all other frequencies, 'X' will be merged last in the Huffman tree construction. It will be one of the two children of the root node, resulting in a code length of exactly 1 bit (0 or 1).

mcq_data.question: In the Interval Partitioning problem (finding the minimum number of rooms for a set of lectures), what is the greedy strategy?

options.A: Sort by finish time and assign to first available room
options.B: Sort by start time and assign to first available room
options.C: Sort by duration and assign to first available room
options.D: Sort by start time and always open a new room

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: For Interval Partitioning, the optimal greedy strategy is to sort intervals by start time. For each interval, check if any room is free (i.e., the last lecture in that room finished before the current lecture starts). If yes, assign it; if no, open a new room. This ensures the minimum number of rooms are used.

mcq_data.question: Does Prim's algorithm work on graphs with negative edge weights?

options.B: Yes, it still finds the MST correctly
options.C: Only if there are no negative cycles
options.D: Only if all weights are transformed to positive values

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Interestingly, both Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms work correctly even if the graph has negative edge weights, provided the goal is to find the MST. The 'greedy' logic of MST relies on the cut property, which doesn't care about the sign of the weights. However, Dijkstra's (for shortest paths) fails with negative weights.

mcq_data.question: What is the primary drawback of using a Greedy algorithm?

options.C: It may not always provide the global optimal solution
options.D: It always has O(2^n) time complexity

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The main disadvantage of the greedy approach is that it is 'shortsighted.' It makes the best local choice without considering future consequences. For many problems (like the 0/1 Knapsack or the Traveling Salesperson Problem), this approach fails to find the absolute best (global) solution.

mcq_data.question: Which algorithm 'grows' the MST from a single starting vertex by adding the nearest unvisited vertex?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Prim's algorithm is a vertex-based greedy approach. It starts from an arbitrary root vertex and expands the spanning tree by adding the minimum weight edge that connects a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside the tree.

mcq_data.question: How many spanning trees can a complete graph with 'n' vertices have?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: This is known as Cayley's Formula. For a complete graph K_n (where every vertex is connected to every other vertex), the total number of distinct spanning trees is n raised to the power of (n - 2). For example, a triangle (n=3) has 3^(3-2) = 3 spanning trees.

mcq_data.question: In the Job Sequencing problem, if the maximum deadline is 'D', what is the maximum number of jobs that can be completed?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Each job takes 1 unit of time. If the furthest deadline for any job is 'D', there are only 'D' time slots available (1, 2, ..., D). Therefore, you can complete at most 'D' jobs, regardless of how many jobs are available.

mcq_data.question: Is the Huffman code for a specific set of frequencies unique?

options.B: No, because the assignment of 0 and 1 to branches is arbitrary
options.C: No, because frequencies change during transmission
options.D: Yes, if the number of characters is even

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The resulting bit lengths for each character are unique in terms of optimality, but the actual bit strings (the codes) are not unique. You can swap '0' and '1' for any left/right branch, or if two nodes have the same frequency, the tree structure itself could vary.

mcq_data.question: What is the time complexity of the Activity Selection problem if the activities are already sorted by finish time?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: If the activities are already sorted by finish time, we only need to iterate through the list once. We pick the first activity, then for every subsequent activity, we check if its start time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the last picked activity. This single pass takes O(n) time.

mcq_data.question: Which statement is TRUE regarding the difference between Kruskal’s and Prim’s algorithms?

options.A: Kruskal’s can result in a disconnected forest during intermediate steps, while Prim’s always maintains a single connected component.
options.B: Prim’s is edge-based while Kruskal’s is vertex-based.
options.C: Kruskal’s is faster for dense graphs.
options.D: Prim's requires the Union-Find data structure.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Kruskal's algorithm adds the smallest edges regardless of where they are in the graph, often creating several small trees (a forest) that eventually merge. Prim's algorithm starts at one node and grows the tree one edge at a time, so the intermediate structure is always a single connected tree.

mcq_data.question: In the Optimal Storage on Tapes problem, how should files be ordered to minimize mean retrieval time?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: To minimize the average time taken to retrieve a file, shorter files should be placed at the beginning of the tape. This is because to reach the n-th file, you must pass over all previous files. Minimizing the length of earlier files reduces the wait time for all subsequent files.

mcq_data.question: Which of the following is NOT a greedy algorithm?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a classic example of a problem that cannot be solved optimally using a greedy approach. It requires Dynamic Programming to consider all weight combinations. In contrast, Huffman Coding, Prim's, and Fractional Knapsack all utilize greedy strategies to achieve optimal solutions.

outro_script.closing: That concludes our 30-question deep dive into Greedy Algorithms. How did you do? If you found some of the graph or Huffman questions tricky, don't worry—these are advanced topics that take practice.

youtube_metadata.description: Master Data Structures and Algorithms with this deep dive into Hashing and Hash Tables. This video covers 30 essential practice questions designed to mimic real-world technical interviews and certification exams. mostsearchedongoogle: What is a hash table in DSA?
How to handle collisions in hash tables
Average time complexity of hash table search
What is a load factor in hashing?

mcq_data.question: What is the primary purpose of a Hash Function in a Hash Table?

options.A: To sort the elements in the table in ascending order.
options.B: To map a large range of keys to a smaller range of indices.
options.C: To increase the storage capacity of the underlying array.
options.D: To ensure that no two keys ever produce the same index.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A hash function is designed to transform a key (which could be a large integer, a string, or an object) into a fixed-size integer value, which serves as an index for the array. This allows the data structure to map a potentially infinite or very large set of keys into a finite number of slots in the hash table, enabling efficient data retrieval.

mcq_data.question: In a well-distributed hash table, what is the average case time complexity for searching for an element?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: One of the most powerful features of hash tables is that, on average, they provide O(1) or constant time complexity for search, insert, and delete operations. This assumes that the hash function distributes keys uniformly across the table and the load factor is kept within a reasonable limit to minimize collisions.

mcq_data.question: Which collision resolution technique uses a linked list at each slot of the hash table?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Chaining (or Separate Chaining) handles collisions by allowing multiple elements to exist at the same index. Each slot in the hash table points to a linked list (or another dynamic container) of all items that hashed to that specific index. This is an 'out-of-table' resolution method.

mcq_data.question: In Linear Probing, if a collision occurs at index 'i', where is the next potential index checked?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Linear Probing is an open-addressing strategy where the algorithm searches for the next available slot sequentially. If index 'i' is occupied, it checks (i+1), then (i+2), and so on, using the modulo operator to wrap around to the beginning of the table if necessary.

mcq_data.question: What does the 'Load Factor' (λ) of a hash table represent?

options.A: The speed of the hash function calculation.
options.B: The ratio of the number of stored elements to the total number of slots.
options.C: The number of collisions that have occurred during insertion.
options.D: The percentage of the table that remains empty.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Load Factor (λ) is defined as n/m, where 'n' is the number of elements currently stored and 'm' is the total number of slots (size) of the hash table. It serves as a measure of how 'full' the table is and is used to decide when to resize (rehash) the table to maintain performance.

mcq_data.question: What is the worst-case time complexity for a search operation in a hash table using Chaining?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In the absolute worst case, all keys could hash to the same index (a 'catastrophic' collision). If this happens in a chaining-based hash table, the data structure effectively becomes a single linked list of length 'n'. Therefore, searching would require traversing all 'n' elements, resulting in O(n) time complexity.

mcq_data.question: Which of the following is a property of a 'Good' Hash Function?

options.A: It should be computationally expensive to prevent hacking.
options.B: It should map all keys to the same index for consistency.
options.C: It should distribute keys uniformly across the table.
options.D: It should return a different value every time it is called for the same key.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A good hash function must be deterministic (same key always gives the same index), fast to compute, and most importantly, it should distribute keys uniformly. Uniform distribution minimizes clusters and collisions, which keeps operations close to O(1).

mcq_data.question: What is a major disadvantage of Linear Probing known as?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Primary Clustering occurs in linear probing because as slots get filled, long runs of occupied slots build up. Any key that hashes into a cluster will require several probes to find an empty slot, and it will also extend the cluster further, progressively degrading performance.

mcq_data.question: In Double Hashing, what is the purpose of the second hash function?

options.A: To compute the initial index for the key.
options.B: To determine the step size for probing when a collision occurs.
options.C: To encrypt the data before it is stored.
options.D: To resize the table when it becomes too full.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Double Hashing reduces clustering by using a second hash function, hash2(key), to determine the probe sequence interval. Instead of a fixed step of 1 (linear) or a growing step (quadratic), the step size depends on the key itself, which helps spread keys more effectively.

mcq_data.question: Which of these is NOT a common application of Hashing?

options.C: Sorting a list of numbers in O(n log n) time.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: While hashing is great for lookups and verification, it is not inherently a sorting algorithm. Standard hashing does not maintain any order of elements. Sorting is typically handled by algorithms like Merge Sort, Quick Sort, or Heap Sort.

mcq_data.question: Quadratic Probing helps to eliminate which problem specifically?

options.D: The need for a hash function

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Quadratic probing eliminates primary clustering (the buildup of long contiguous segments in the table) by using a quadratic function to find the next slot. However, it can still suffer from secondary clustering, where keys that hash to the same initial index follow the same probe sequence.

mcq_data.question: When a hash table is resized (Rehashing), why can't we just copy the old array elements to the first half of the new array?

options.B: The hash function is based on the table size; indices will change.
options.C: The data would become corrupted during the copy.
options.D: The new array must be empty to start with.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Most hash functions use the formula `index = hash(key) % table_size`. When the `table_size` changes during resizing, the index for every existing key must be recalculated. If you simply copied them, you would never find the elements again using the new table size.

mcq_data.question: Which collision resolution technique is considered 'Closed Hashing'?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Open Addressing is often called 'Closed Hashing' because all elements are stored within the hash table (the array) itself. No elements are stored outside in separate structures like linked lists, which is the case in Open Hashing (Chaining).

mcq_data.question: In a Chaining-based hash table, what is the expected length of a chain if there are 'n' elements and 'm' slots?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Under the assumption of simple uniform hashing, each key is equally likely to hash to any of the 'm' slots. Therefore, the expected number of keys in any given slot is simply the total number of keys divided by the total number of slots, which is n/m (the load factor λ).

mcq_data.question: Why is the size of a hash table often chosen to be a Prime Number?

options.A: Because prime numbers use less memory.
options.B: To reduce the number of collisions when using the division method.
options.C: To make the hash function run faster.
options.D: To ensure that the load factor is always less than 1.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: When using the division method (key % table_size), if the table size is a power of 2 or a composite number, certain patterns in the input keys might lead to heavy collisions. Using a prime number that is not close to a power of 2 helps distribute keys more uniformly across the table.

mcq_data.question: In an Open Addressing hash table, how is an element 'deleted' so that search still works?

options.A: The slot is set back to NULL immediately.
options.B: The slot is marked with a special 'Deleted' flag (tombstone).
options.C: The entire table is rehashed immediately.
options.D: Elements are shifted back to fill the hole.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: In open addressing, if you simply set a deleted slot to NULL, you might break a probe sequence. A search for a later element in the sequence would stop at the NULL slot and fail to find the element. Using a 'tombstone' tells the search algorithm to keep looking, but tells the insert algorithm that the slot is available.

mcq_data.question: What is 'Perfect Hashing'?

options.A: A hash function that never has a collision for a specific static set of keys.
options.B: A hash function that produces indices in alphabetical order.
options.C: A hash table that has a load factor of exactly 1.0.
options.D: A hash table that uses O(n^2) space to ensure O(1) search.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Perfect hashing is a technique used when the set of keys is static (fixed and known in advance). A perfect hash function maps each key to a unique index with zero collisions. This is often implemented using a two-level hashing scheme to achieve O(1) worst-case search time.

mcq_data.question: When hashing strings, what is the 'Polynomial Rolling Hash' primarily used for?

options.A: To compress strings into smaller sizes.
options.B: To efficiently compute hash values for substrings (like in Rabin-Karp).
options.C: To sort strings by their ASCII values.
options.D: To encrypt strings for secure storage.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Polynomial rolling hashing allows for the computation of a hash for a sliding window of a string in O(1) time after an initial O(k) setup. This is the foundation of the Rabin-Karp string matching algorithm.

mcq_data.question: What is the space complexity of a Hash Table storing 'n' elements using Chaining with 'm' slots?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The space complexity is O(n + m) because you need 'm' slots for the array (the buckets) and 'n' nodes for the total elements stored in the linked lists across all buckets.

mcq_data.question: In Java, what is the default initial capacity and load factor for a HashMap?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Java's `java.util.HashMap` defaults to an initial capacity of 16 and a load factor of 0.75. This is considered a good balance between time and space costs for general-purpose usage.

mcq_data.question: What happens in a Hash Table if the hash function is `h(k) = 1` for all keys?

options.A: The table will be very fast because the index is constant.
options.B: The table will function like a Linked List (if using chaining).
options.C: The table will throw an Overflow exception.
options.D: The table will automatically resize to accommodate the keys.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: If every key hashes to the same value, all elements will be placed in the same bucket. In a chaining-based implementation, this creates one long linked list, turning O(1) operations into O(n) operations.

mcq_data.question: Which of the following ensures that Linear Probing will eventually visit every slot in the table?

options.A: The table size is a prime number.
options.C: The step size is 1 and the table size is at least 'n'.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Linear probing moves in steps of 1. As long as the step size (1) and the table size 'm' are relatively prime (which they always are since 1 divides everything), and there is at least one empty slot, the probe will visit every slot.

mcq_data.question: What is 'Universal Hashing'?

options.A: A hash function that works for every possible data type.
options.B: Choosing a hash function randomly from a carefully designed family of functions.
options.C: A hash function that produces the same output on all operating systems.
options.D: A hash function that uses the entire universe of keys.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Universal Hashing involves picking a hash function at random from a family of hash functions at the start of execution. This prevents an adversary from choosing a 'bad' set of keys that specifically cause many collisions for a known, fixed hash function.

mcq_data.question: How does increasing the table size (m) typically affect the number of collisions?

options.A: It increases collisions because there is more space to collide.
options.B: It decreases collisions because the load factor (n/m) decreases.
options.C: It has no effect on collisions.
options.D: It makes collisions more expensive to resolve.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: By increasing 'm', the load factor λ = n/m decreases. A lower load factor means the table is more sparse, which mathematically reduces the probability that two keys will hash to the same index.

mcq_data.question: What is the advantage of using a Self-Balancing Binary Search Tree instead of a Linked List for Chaining?

options.B: It improves worst-case search time from O(n) to O(log n) within a bucket.
options.C: It makes the hash function easier to write.
options.D: It prevents the need for rehashing.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Some modern implementations (like Java 8's HashMap) switch from a linked list to a balanced tree (like a Red-Black Tree) when a bucket exceeds a certain threshold. This ensures that even under heavy collisions, the search time in that bucket is O(log k) rather than O(k).

mcq_data.question: Which of these is a 'One-Way' property of cryptographic hash functions?

options.A: It is easy to find a key from its hash value.
options.B: It is computationally infeasible to reverse the hash to find the original key.
options.C: The hash value is always the same length as the input key.
options.D: Two different keys should always produce the same hash.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: A 'One-Way' (pre-image resistance) property means that given a hash value 'h', it is practically impossible to find the input 'x' such that Hash(x) = h. This is vital for security applications like password storage.

mcq_data.question: If we insert elements 10, 20, 30, 40 into a hash table of size 10 using Linear Probing and h(k) = k % 10, what happens?

options.A: They all go into index 0 using chaining.
options.C: They all overwrite each other at index 0.
options.D: The table throws an error because the keys are multiples of the size.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: All keys (10, 20, 30, 40) have a remainder of 0 when divided by 10. 10 goes to index 0. 20 collides at 0, probes to 1. 30 collides at 0 and 1, probes to 2. 40 collides at 0, 1, and 2, and probes to 3.

mcq_data.question: What is 'Cuckoo Hashing'?

options.A: A method where an element can be stored in one of two locations.
options.B: A method where elements are deleted randomly.
options.C: A method where hash functions change every minute.
options.D: A method used only for bird migration data.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Cuckoo hashing uses two hash functions and two tables. An element can be at index h1(key) in table 1 or h2(key) in table 2. If both are full, it 'kicks out' an existing element to its alternative location, potentially triggering a chain of displacements. It provides O(1) worst-case lookup time.

mcq_data.question: What is 'Consistent Hashing' primarily used for?
mcq_data.detailedexplanation: Consistent hashing is used in distributed systems so that when a new node is added or removed from a cluster, only a small fraction of keys (k/n) need to be remapped. This prevents a total system re-shuffle, which would happen with standard `key % n` hashing.

mcq_data.question: What is the Birthday Paradox's relevance to Hashing?

options.A: It calculates the age of the hash table.
options.B: It shows that collisions are much more likely than intuitively expected.
options.C: It proves that hashing is impossible for large datasets.
options.D: It determines the best day to perform rehashing.

mcq_data.detailedexplanation: The Birthday Paradox shows that in a room of just 23 people, there's a 50% chance two share a birthday. In hashing, this implies that collisions occur much sooner than one might think, even if the table is relatively empty and the hash function is good.

Topics Covered:
